author: hoeschec
text:
I am learning that knowing the target of an engulf is as important (if not more important) than knowing EG VS FO.

An engulf is only useful/valid/ if it's target is unmet.

I found a really good example on EUR-JPY

This is a really long example, because I am going step by step for identifying the target. I don't think we spend enough time stressing the importance of finding targets

There are 12 charts posted total (over the next two posts) and it is step by step to show the phases of analysis. I hope this is organized enough to follow...if not, please don't hesitate to ask for clarifications

First chart shows the initial FL Boxes that got me interested in this area. FL Box C engulfs the low of FL Box A, and as a result, forms a swap zone.

Before analyzing the details of FL Box C to find a place to get short, I must find out where the target is located for this engulf. I need to find the target for shorts. I look left and see an area with lots of PA that exists before FL Box A. This is an area of consolidation where price eventually broke to the upside and formed FL Box A.

If I am looking for a target for shorts, I need to find the last opposing bullish controlled swap zone....

This next chart zooms in to this area (previously inside the neon colored circle in the chart above). Start drawing FL Boxes - only the important ones that held price AND as a result price made a new low/high. We only want the strongest zones. I found two main zones: the blue rectangle shows an area of bullish/buyer control, and the long black rectangle shows an area of very strong seller control.

Look how well price respects the upper level of the black rectangle....it takes a while to break this high. This is good - it means this is a strong bearish controlled zone. When price breaks this upper level, it will be significant.

When looking for a target for shorts, we want to find the swap zone that gives us true demand...remember on my previous posts I said "The best place to sell is in an area that is a target for longs".It works the other way too "The best place to buy is in an area that is also a target for sells". This true demand is the origin of the move up, and it is the 'magnet' that is attracting price from above. This 'magnet attraction' concept is something Salivan came up with and it makes a lot of sense.

Wait for the break of the strong bearish controlled rectangle. Here is when details matter...don't be sloppy/lazy with your analysis.

Just because price breaks the upper level of the strong bear-controlled rectangle (FL Box), doesn't mean it is the best place to draw your new Fl Box. Look for the following:

** Wait for price to break your important zone. After the break, label the breaks and the corresponding lows that form.

Look at these breaks and corresponding Lows: Pick the lowest low that forms and find the high that preceded the lowest low. These two points make up you new FL Box..the important Fl Box that holds the true demand and origin of the move up. You want to choose the high the corresponds to the last low that forms because you want to origin of the move up...it has to be the last demand zone before price moves up.

The chart below shows this new FL Box D. This Fl Box holds the origin of the move up.

Here is a clean chart showing all of the important components of finding the target for this EUR-JPY trade:

More to follow on the next post....

author: hoeschec
text:
This is a continuation from a long post that started above (post # 1101). You might want to read post #1101 first, as it will be easier to follow along with this post. These concepts are really hard to explain using words, so hopefully it isn't too confusing...

Referring to FL Box D: We know this FL Box holds to origin of the move up, therefore it is our target for shorts. Of course, we need to refine the target to an exact FL.Here is how I did that:

If you read my posts last night on post #1094 and #1096, you will see I use the same 3 data point method for identifying the important areas within FL Box D. Whether you are looking for a place to enter the market, or for a place to exit the market, the analysis is the same. We want true supply/demand areas that are origins and targets.

I use this analysis in FL Box D to find true demand...true demand = origin of the move up = the target for my shorts.

Target Data Point 1: Is the engulf of the strong bearish controlled FL Box

Target Data Point 2: Is the FTR/FL that forms the extreme end of FL Box D. True demand is located here as well as the MPL

Target Data Point 3: This is where price makes a new high, which confirms FL Box D. This is a DBR.

The next chart shows a zoomed in view of Fl Box D. To ID the true demand zone, we start drawing LTF swap zones...only the most important ones. Find the first swap zone that forms that still has FOF.

You can see where this LTF swap zone first occurs. This level is strengthened by also containing a perfect looking DP. True demand with a nicely formed DP = great place to attract sellers. I drew FL Box E (within FL Box D) to narrow the target down. I copied a neon greed dotted line (the line runs horizontally through FL Box E) to show the exact location where price bounced later on. You can see exactly where the confirmed target was...it reacted exactly in this area.

The next chart shows a bird's eye view of the entire trade, with the target extended along the bottom of the chart so you can see how price reacts to it, as it falls from FL Box C after the major engulf of FL Box A.

Now I will focus on the entry... the PA located inside Fl Box C will give us true supply & the origin of the move down. You don't start looking for an entry until you identify the target of your engulf and determine that the target is still unmet.

There is an important distinction to make (regarding this specific example) about the target being hit before price returns to the true supply level in FL Box C, but i'll discuss that towards the end

Here is the same three point analysis:

Data Point 1: Price engulfs Fl Box A - this is a major engulf and is the reason we are even looking at this EUR-JPY example. The target we just found is the target of this engulf.

Data Point 2: This is the extreme edge of FL Box C and is also the FTR/FL and true supply. MPL is located here too.

Data Point 3: Price makes a lower low which confirms FL Box C. This is a RBD.

The next chart shows a zoomed in view if FL Box C. We are looking for the first swap zone that forms that still has FOF. LTF FL Boxes are drawn and you can see a nice supply zone with another perfect DP. This zone is also the origin of the move down. You can see how well price reacts to this level on its FTB. Finding nicely formed DP's in your true supply/demand level really increases the odds that price will be attracted.

Now..for the most important part of this whole example: As you can see in the chart below, price broke out of FL Box C and hit the target straightaway without returning to true supply. In a situation like this, you would want to be very careful about shorting at the FTB to true supply, because the engulf has already hit its target. If you weren't aware that the target had already been hit, you might go short and place a stop above the MPL of true supply....depending on where your limit order was placed you would be stopped out (see the big red circle). Often times, I think failed trades are a result of not knowing where your target is located, after an engulf occurs. This becomes even more important when you start looking at higher time frames and drilling down on many different scales and time frames.

Getting in on a trade, in the right scale, because of an engulf that has an unmet target, will drastically increase the odds that your trade works out.

I notice originally formed areas of FOF, that have engulfs that met their targets, are highly reactive when price reacts on its FTB.

Has anyone else seen this? Is this what Salivan means when he asks "where is price coming from?"

Here is a 4-hour chart of AUD-CAD:

The areas circled in green are originally formed areas of FOF. I have marked three of these zones. The areas marked with a red circle are reactions to the FOF.

Zone 1 is originally formed FOF, and hits its target. Since the target was hit, when price returns to Zone 1, it will bounce.

Zone 2 is originally formed FOF, and its target is Zone 1.

(Reaction # 2 is a trading opportunity as a FTB to Zone 1, and it is also meeting the target for Zone 2, which makes zone 2 a good place to trade when price returns on its FTB)

Zone 3 is originally formed FOF, and hits its target (Zone 2).

(Reaction # 3 is a trading opportunity as a FTB to Zone 2, and it is also meeting the target for Zone 3, which makes Zone 3 a good place to trade when price returns on its FTB).

author: hoeschec
text:
Something I am still really struggling with is identifying true supply/demand zones and targets. It's something that I can find on historical charts, because I can look back at the PA and track where price reacted/bounced/engulfed etc... But... successful trading requires us to ID these zones in real time.

Some zones are easy to ID...for example, like this one:

Very nicely formed high with a clear engulf and FTR/DP formed. Clear price reactions and nice momentum out of the zone. Simple and logical.

Just as I am feeling more confident, I come upon this monster:

Not as clear...

Now, assuming this is real time, here is how I would try to ID the true supply zone:

Swap zone formed, important EG. This would be my interpretation of FOF/origin of the move down/future target for longs.

As you can see, I would have been wrong. The actual zone appears to be located above the level I marked. What makes this level important? I see the nice DP that exists, but that didn't form as a result of an important engulf of an opposing swap zone...

I know price sometimes forms a FO to the DP above a true supply zone, but how are we supposed to trade if there is always a risk of a FO to a level above? There is almost always some type of DP above an area of FOF. In this case, price dropped from the origin and hit its target. Since price hit its target, the origin is a good place to trade a bounce when price RT on its FTB. Trading the bounce on the wrong area of true supply would be a loss.

author: hoeschec
text:
With regard to price faking out past true supply to a DP located above (see my last post for a chart example and the drawing below for reference)

What I am trying to understand:

In a scenario where price forms a FO to the DP above true supply:

Does a DP located above true supply negate the the true supply zone itself with regard to FOF, or do we view it as price skipping over true supply? If true supply = FOF, and we know FOF bounces price, how can price just "jump" over this important zone to hit a DP above? It makes no sense to me.... Doesn't price have to pass through this zone of fresh orders? The only way to blow through an important area of FOF to a DP above would be to flood the market with so many buy orders that the FOF (sell orders in this example) doesn't turn price. What would be the point of doing that, if the goal is to drop price? If you want to drop price, you want someone else to start buying from you...by pushing price through an area of FOF short orders you absorb the liquidity at that level by buying more orders than actually exist at the level (that would be the only way to physically push through that level...right?). Only IT's have the financial power to push price on such a huge scale, and it would be a very expensive move to make to hit a DP.

The only way this becomes profitable for the IT is if there are so many sell orders/liquidity/FOF in the DP above, it warrants the buying that is necessary to push price to this level. There would have to be more FOF in the DP than exists in the true supply zone below it. Under what circumstances does a DP have more FOF than a true supply level below it, and how can we identify this on a chart? Is this the key to predicting when a FO will occur?
